    来自中国电网的超级气候污染物正在炙烤地球
    Read this article in English. 中国的电网有一个肮脏的秘密：尽管它在可再生能源发展引领全球，它也是地球上最强效温室气体的最大排放源。 六氟化硫（SF6）是一种合成化学物质，在高压设备中作为电气绝缘介质发挥着至关重要的角色。这种气体无色无味、无毒、且不可燃。但它也是气候杀手，按等质量计算，其使地球变暖的效力是二氧化碳的24,300倍。一旦释放，六氟化硫会在大气中存留1,000年。 排放主要来自电力行业。该行业中将这种气体用于断路器和其他高压设备中，以防止电弧放电。六氟化硫几乎无法被破坏，是任何现代电网的关键安全屏障，确保电力只在需要时流向所需之处。然而，当中国的电气设备达到使用寿命终点时，其中大部分的气体很可能被排放到大气中。 早在2014年，中国政府研究员就警告称，六氟化硫“对全球环境构成重大潜在威胁”。然而，这种气候污染物的排放在中国仍是未受监管的。 中国生态环境部最近表示，中国电力企业当前回收—或有能力回收—其废弃六氟化硫气体的90%。然而，Inside Climate News估算，实际回收率要低得多，仅为30%。这些企业只需付出很低的成本，就能将回收率提高到约90%，从而大幅减少温室气体排放。 该分析参考了数百页的政府文件、中国主要电力企业的年度报告、经同行评审的研究，以及对数十位学者和政策专家的采访。根据这项评估，Inside Climate News估算，中国国有的输配电企业每年可将从电气设备中回收的六氟化硫量增加约1,400吨。这样做有望减少中国所有行業该污染物的总排放量近三分之一，预计每年成本约为600万美元，这仅占中国每年投资电网约700亿美元的一小部分。 如果把这种气体排放到大气，而不是将其回收，那简直就是一场三级火警，美国环境保护署前含氟温室气体排放分析师黛博拉·奥廷格在谈到Inside Climate News的评估时说道…

    The Guardian view on the Nepal-Tibet floods: a spur to action on climate | Editorial
    New research links last month’s disaster to fossil fuel pollution. Supporting disaster-hit countries must be at the centre of climate politics Following a familiar pattern, coverage of the glacier collapse on the Nepal-Tibet border three weeks ago has subsided with the initial shock. But while the world’s attention has shifted, Nepal remains in the midst of an appalling tragedy. As well as at least 1,300 people who are known to have been killed, more than 5,000 are missing, some of them trapped in tunnels linked to the 13 hydropower plants that were damaged by the floods. On Wednesday four bodies were recovered from one of these tunnels, with searches ongoing. Families of the missing people are desperate for news. Last week the country’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, said that it would ask the UN’s loss and damage fund for $20m (£15m) towards a total rebuilding cost of around $5bn (£3.75bn) – including the replacement of up to 20,000 homes. The first academic study linking the disaster to the climate crisis will now be added to that application. Scientists at Imperial College London, along with international collaborators on the World Weather Attribution project, found that a number of drivers of the glacier fall had been made worse by atmospheric heating. While not the sole cause, fossil fuel pollution was judged to have destabilised the geology of the mountain environment. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?     Trump’s love of fossil fuels is about more than money | Moira Donegan

In fact, the disparity is greater than this catchy phrasing suggests: there are actually more yoga instructors in the US than there are people employed in the entirety of the coalmining industry, miners and otherwise. It’s not even especially close: about 38,000 people in the US work in coal, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics, compared to about 100,000 yoga instructors who are registered with the Yoga Alliance, an industry group. If you looked only at the numbers, you might think a politician would be incentivized to talk about the interests of the yoga industry, about the dignity that yoga jobs give to American families, or about the need to foster growth in the yoga industry, more than they talk about these things for coal; after all, yoga, not coal, is putting food on the table in more American households. But no politician would ever talk about the interests of yoga teachers, or wax poetic about their role in the American dream, the way they do with coal miners; if they did, they’d be laughed out of the room. And we all know why: yoga is thought of as decadent, cosmopolitan and feminine, while coal mining is imagined as hardscrabble, honorable and masculine. Rhode Island is the second state to ban that practice Jeannine Johansen remembers the halcyon days of Woonsocket, Rhode Island, when so many of its steep streets were punctuated by grocery stores: Almacs, A&P, Piggly Wiggly and Star Market. In the blizzard of 1978, “everybody went to Fernandes [Produce] because Stop & Shop was too far, and all the roads were closed, so we had to walk”, said the native Woonsocketer. These days, Woonsocket is down to one full-service supermarket: a solitary Price Rite serving 45,000 residents, 37% of them food insecure, perched at the top of a hill in a strip mall at the edge of the city. A nearby Dollar General offers frozen meat and packaged foods.
